HCBCOGN312.name: Psycholinguistics
HCBCOGN312.contribution: Studies speech comprehension and production, acquisition, bilingualism and language impairments from cognitive and neurobiological perspectives.
HCBCOGN312.topics: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.

candidateDecisions.label: Language learning and teaching across the lifespan
candidateDecisions.reason: Psycholinguistics includes acquisition and bilingualism, and Rhetoric in Action includes coaching children in public speaking. Lifespan psychology offers a broader developmental perspective. Together these do not establish a sequence in acquiring and teaching additional languages.

candidateDecisions.label: Celtic literatures and linguistics
candidateDecisions.reason: World Myth & Literature provides cross-cultural study of texts and traditions. UCR has no sustained sequence in Celtic languages, medieval Celtic textual traditions or historical grammar.

analysis: The closest composition adds comparative myth, epic and reception plus applied rhetoric and community coaching to a literary sequence covering close reading, world literature, autobiography, film adaptation and independent interpretation. Style & Meaning applies morphology, syntax and register to literary and other texts. Psycholinguistics contributes direct study of acquisition, bilingualism and speech processing, supported by the brain and behaviour prerequisite. Neither gives the full sequence in English phonetic transcription, language history, grammar or dialect variation. Rhetoric gives genuine written and oral argument and revision opportunities; it does not replace a specialist English writing lab. Modern history and histories of gender support cultural interpretation, while the American Century research seminar contributes source criticism and an independent historical paper. The second composition adds media archaeology, environmental media, documentary history and production, Western art history and advanced art-historical writing, developing the shared literature and film core into research on transformation between forms. The third combines comparative politics, modern and contemporary social theory, media representation and Indigenous history, with qualitative methods and stylistics. Psycholinguistics supports language processing, but global cultural coverage comes primarily from identity and representation, not a survey of World Englishes. The language acquisition candidate was tested against Psycholinguistics, Lifespan Developmental Psychology, and public speaking coaching in Rhetoric in Action. These courses give meaningful fragments but do not form a language pedagogy and second-language acquisition sequence. Myth, literature and historical courses give comparative approaches without sustained Celtic language study or medieval Celtic textual interpretation.

alignment.rationale: Utrecht studies English Renaissance literature as a dedicated period. UCR Introduction to Literary Studies teaches close reading across genres and periods.
Both connect texts to historical and cultural change. UCR studies a wider world canon, with works beyond the English-language period studied at Utrecht.
Utrecht studies English-language literature from 1850 to 1950 in a dedicated course. UCR studies modernist narration and subjectivity within its broader literature courses.
UCR embeds research preparation across methods and advanced courses rather than providing a directly equivalent dedicated Thesis Lab.
Utrecht teaches phonetic transcription and pronunciation. UCR Psycholinguistics examines how speech is processed and produced.
Both develop argument and attention to the audience. Utrecht emphasises writing and revision, while UCR studies rhetoric in written and spoken discourse.
Both examine grammar and language choices. UCR uses morphology, syntax and register to explain stylistic effects.
Utrecht studies the historical development of languages in the British Isles. UCR Psycholinguistics studies language processing and acquisition.
UCR offers linguistics, stylistics and psycholinguistics contributions but no dedicated morphosyntax course.
Utrecht studies Old English in its early medieval setting. UCR offers cross-cultural textual interpretation and broader historical study.
UCR studies identity and language across communication, sociology and media rather than in one dedicated course.
UCR offers social and communication analysis but no full sociolinguistics-of-Englishes course.
UCR provides global cultural and communication perspectives but no dedicated World Englishes course.
The selected Utrecht specialisation requires Topics in Linguistics. UCR covers stylistics and psycholinguistics in separate courses.
Both develop empirical research design and statistical analysis. The UCR course also introduces qualitative and experimental approaches.
This is genuine elective/profile space and is preserved without inventing content.
Utrecht requires an individual thesis in English Language and Culture. UCR offers optional independent research alongside advanced course projects.
